scope: A geographic introduction to selected regions of Athenian coin circulation and related owl-type production. Not an exhaustive mint or findspot map.

sourcesAdded.title: The circulation and distribution of classical Greek coinage
sourcesAdded.author: Zane Mullins
sourcesAdded.scope: Hoard-based distribution of Classical Greek coinages, including Athenian coins in Egypt, the Levant, Mesopotamia, Iran and Afghanistan, and discussion of foreign imitations.
sourcesAdded.note: The sample covers 550–300 BCE, not every period or every find. Some older hoard descriptions combine Athens and imitations. Hoard locations do not reconstruct exact trade routes; use, issuing intent and movement mechanisms remain interpretive questions.

sourcesAdded.title: Hoards and Overstrikes: The Numismatic Evidence
sourcesAdded.author: Margaret Thompson · Penn Museum, Expedition 21(4)
sourcesAdded.scope: Published hoard evidence for Athenian coins in Sicily, southwest Anatolia, Egypt, the Levant and farther east; discussion of coins used as bullion.
sourcesAdded.note: A historical synthesis retained for its documented geographic examples. Its chronology and broad attribution arguments are not automatically adopted; later research, including Gentelli et al. (2026), revisits some eastern imitations. This overview is not a complete gazetteer of finds.

sourcesAdded.title: Mazaces, Babylon · Le Rider 1997 pseudo-atheniens 10
sourcesAdded.author: IRIS / University of Oxford
sourcesAdded.scope: An Athena–owl type attributed to Mazaces and the mint of Babylon, in Babylonia.
sourcesAdded.note: IRIS gives this type a broad 350–300 BCE range. The geographic introduction uses the mint attribution; it does not extend this date range to every Babylonian owl-type coin or imply an exact issue date. No new specimen photograph is embedded.

map.transformation: Land polygons clipped to the bounds and projected linearly into a 900 × 590 SVG. No modern borders or inferred coin routes. Coordinates are editorial label anchors for broad regions, except Athens city.
map.presentationNote: The overview spans thousands of kilometres. Geographic coordinates and coastline geometry are unchanged. Place names are offset, connectors stop outside label bounds, and markers are enlarged for visibility. Label spacing and marker size are not distance or area scales.

limits: Findspots and regional hoard evidence must not be treated as exact mint locations or complete travel histories.
Current coastlines are orientation only; ancient shorelines and political boundaries are not reconstructed.
Regional imitation attribution is not assumed for every eastern find. The 2026 reattribution caveat remains visible.
Existing 28 sources, 17 image records and all BnF rights flags remain; three geographical sources are appended.
